In fact the Government of Canada is committed to the negotiation and settlement of land claims in all parts of Canada where we can be persuaded that there is a legitimate claim.

Mr. Speaker, some farmers are very concerned about the results of the current GATT negotiations.
Yesterday I met with representatives of several supply management organizations, all of whom expressed their support for Canada's proposals for strengthening and clarifying article XI of GATT. They are concerned that Canada will be forced to abandon its firm stand on article XI in order to reach a compromise between all parties.
My question is for the Minister of Agriculture. Can the minister assure this House of his commitment to a strengthened and clarified article XI?

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member's question is appropriate because at this time there are unjustified fears.
The Government of Canada developed its position at GATT with the stakeholders, with the farmers and with the producers. That position is to maintain, to strengthen and to clarify article XI. That means that Canada, the government along with the producers, will maintain that position on supply management throughout the negotiations. We have stated that before.
I have stated that not only has Canada said we would maintain it. I have actively been promoting the position of clarification and strengthening of article XI wherever I have had the opportunity to meet members of GATT.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a week ago Dominion Textiles announced that it was shutting down its Hawkesbury Fiberworld plant laying off permanently another 86 workers, stating that it could no longer compete with U.S. plants because of the high dollar policy of this government.
Given that this is the second plant closure in two weeks for the same reason in my riding, how many more plants have to be closed and how many more people have to lose their jobs before this government understands the disaster that its high dollar policy is causing to my constituents and others?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member blames the ills of the textile industry in his riding on the value of the dollar. I would like to see that rationale.
October 28, 1991

Perhaps the hon. member may want to share some of the information with me because quite frankly, as has been pointed out on many occasions, you cannot devalue your way to prosperity in this country. One has to compete in the international marketplace, the global marketplace. Many industries in fact are doing just that.
I think the merchandise trade balance surplus which is growing is a clear indication that Canadian companies are indeed competing.
The hon. member should know that the value of the Canadian dollar over the last 40 years was 92.6 cents. Today the dollar is in the 88-cent range, considerably below the 92.6-cent average which was the prevailing average over the 40-year period.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are not talking about 40 years ago. We are talking about people who are losing their jobs today.

I would like to direct my supplementary to the Minister of State (Small Businesses). Eastern Ontario is being hard hit as a result of unemployment rates of up to 15 per cent in Hawkesbury, 16 per cent in Cornwall and similar rates in Pembroke and other parts of the region.
When will the minister announce a recovery program for Eastern Ontario which is suffering as a result of the policies of his government and his Minister of Finance, who refuse to listen?

speakeroldname: Hon. Tom Hockin (Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member and I have discussed this at length over the past few months. He knows that we are preparing a program which will address eastern Ontario in particular.
One thing that he should notice is that he has agreed with me in the past that what is needed is a more
Oral Questions
competitive environment in eastern Ontario. A lot of this has to do with training. A lot of this has to do with a more productive labour force, and that is part of the prosperity discussions and consultations that we are going to be beginning with shortly. I hope the hon. member will join in those discussions.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of State for Fitness and Amateur Sport.
This weekend in Victoria there was the national coaching seminar at which 151 coaches signed a petition expressing their deep concern with the removal of Abby Hoffman from her position and in particular the timing, which was four months before the winter Olympics and nine months before the summer Olympics. speakeroldname: Hon. Pierre H. Cadieux (Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport) and Minister of State (Youth) and Deputy Leader of the Government in the House of Commons):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport); Minister of State (Youth); Deputy Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader

On the other hand, I was informed about the concerns with respect to high performance sports, which I addressed very specifically in a speech I gave to Sports Forum II the night before I left for Victoria and at which my hon. friend was present. Routine Proceedings POINT OF ORDER

speakeroldname: Hon. Benoit Bouchard (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:

speechtext: So I see that there is no unanimous consent for now. I therefore ask hon. members on both sides of the House to get together to move the situation forward.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was really trying to point out some of the inadequacies that have come along with regard to the government and Canada Post in dealing with a potential powder keg that they have had over a very long period of time.
Through the seven years this government has been in power we have seen a decline in the relationship of the employee and the employer situation at Canada Post and a decline in most of labour's problems as far as the government is concerned.
Where have these energies been placed? Obviously there has been some concern over the last while with regard to Canada Post and its approach to public relations. It seems to me that the greatest public relations goal that Canada Post could have carried out would have been to set something in place which would give its employees some confidence, some esteem, some good feelings about the corporation. It has not chosen to go in that direction. It clearly has chosen to take other action.
One of the actions that many people in my riding have been very upset about is removing the word "Canada" from Canada Post. We no longer have the word "Canada" there. I guess that is the course of privatization, but it also is the course of disassociation of this government from Canada Post. That is veiy unfortunate because this government is still responsible for that service.
As my colleagues have stated many, many times, the removal of the word "Canada" from Canada Post is a removal of a symbol that all Canadians did cherish and it is something that should not have happened.
We have seen it pursuing sponsorships like a SkyDome box. We have seen it sending out advertising in areas of the arts and car racing, rather than getting down to the nitty-gritty and dealing with its employees in some positive fashion.
While it is advertising and renting boxes at the SkyDome, it is receiving over 100,000 complaints about what is happening within the corporation.
I received several copies of video promotions which were sent to the employees about how great the Canada Post Corporation was. Those video reports came back to me, telling me what negative action Canada Post and this government were taking with regard to dealing with the employees.
As a matter of fact the promotions were causing exactly the opposite, negative reactions from its employees. The result is that many of the things it is doing, bragging about the profits, its advertising, renting boxes at the SkyDome, are causing the employees to ask: "Why does it not treat us relatively fairly. Why does it not sit down and negotiate a contract that would be reasonable for us?" Canada Post has stepped aside. Over the last two years while the employees have been working without a contract, the government has totally avoided pursuing this issue and getting things straightened out.
What has happened as far as the service area is concerned? If we really believe that service to Canadians is the priority of Canada Post, why have we seen 1,000

*
*mnm
October 28, 1991

post office closures in the last couple of years? Why have we seen door to door delivery stopped and supermailboxes put in their place? Why are seniors, who at one time received mail at their homes, now travelling somewhere else to pick up their daily deliveries? Certainly, that creates a tremendous hardship and at the same time it created a great deal of tension between management and the employees.
Two levels of service to Canadians is a hallmark of this government's approach to Canada Post.
If the bottom line really were service, then it would not have taken the approach it has over the last seven years. It certainly would have looked at the situation of its workers and handled it much differently.
Watching seniors line up this summer highlighted in my mind the attitudes of Canada Post and this government toward the workers they employ.
I was questioned about the long lines seniors experienced and the difficulties they had in collecting cheques. In the 100 degree temperatures, many people were unable to stand in line over long periods of time and it was very distressing to these individuals.
I phoned Canada Post and talked to the executives there and suggested that CUPW had recommended that they would take those cheques, deliver them to seniors and make sure the system operated properly. The answer that I got back from Canada Post showed the difficulty that exists. Management in Canada Post suggested that the workers could not be trusted to deliver the cheques and therefore they were not taking action at that time.
The next day, Liberals in our caucus got together and discussed the issue and demanded that the government accept the suggestion of Canada Post and that the minister pursue what CUPW had suggested.
We then sent a letter to the minister and had a press conference in order to bring this item out to the public. The result was that the minister did act and accepted CUPW's request. I will commend him for that, but the minister should have been involved with that much sooner rather than sitting back.
At the same time, we made a recommendation to the minister that, instead of allowing this process to deteriorate as it had, he to appoint a mediator and make certain that the hearings on both sides were handled reasonably well.
Government Orders
The minister at that point again responded to Liberal recommendations. He came out that evening suggesting that he would appoint a mediator. It was two days later that he appointed Alan Gold as the mediator in the dispute. But I want you to realize that the Liberal Party is not just sitting back criticizing. We have made very positive recommendations as to how this minister and this government can move along with the process rather than totally sitting back, ignoring the situation and allowing it to deteriorate.
I believe that the mediation that has gone forward with Mr. Gold, CUPW and Canada Post is very positive. I understand that a little earlier today, CUPW gave Canada Post notice that it may possibly go out on strike as early as tomorrow. That creates another disastrous situation.
But the government seems to move step after step after step to add to the turmoil, the tension and the real causes rather than tiy to resolve issues and create a better climate for all to work under.
It is the government's responsibility to look at the causes of tension, to look at the difficulties and not just bluntly say: "Take it or leave it, this is the way it is". I believe that is why this government over seven years has developed such difficulties with all of its workers and not just CUPW workers. If we look at all of the workers who serve this government and labour across this country, it is very, very downtrodden. Jobs have been lost, anger raised and there has been almost a rebellion in the land. What is causing it? I believe it is this government's inaction to deal properly and fairly with the work force of this country.
It is important that this government take that on.
I will reiterate again that no one in this country, in the Liberal Party, in the Conservative Party or the NDP Party wants to see a strike or the disruption of the vital service Canada Post offers. It is the responsibility of this government to make certain that the tensions and problems that have generated over the last seven years are dealt with and dealt with adequately and properly.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
subtopic: POSTAL SERVICES CONTINUATION ACT, 1991 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity this afternoon to speak to Bill C-40, whose purpose is to force Canadian postal workers back to work.

How did we get into this mess? The government across the way of course will say it is the fault of Jean-Claude Parrot or of anybody else who happens to disagree with the government. That is the standard Tory line.
It is not that simple. First of all let us remember that in 1986 the government across the way approved the corporate plan of Canada Post. So Canada Post's approach to management, the broad concept that it is aiming at right now has been approved by this government. No one forced the minister to approve that corporate plan. I did not see Jean-Claude Parrot successfully twisting the arm of the minister in order to have the corporate plan changed, nor was the opposition able to convince the government to do otherwise.

Government Orders
As far as I remember the only person who managed to get a small element of the corporate plan changed was a lone backbencher on the government side. In 1986 he started a caucus revolt on the issue of the threat by Canada Post whereby rural mail would be eliminated except for main county roads. All the boxes would have to be repatriated along those main roads and there would be no delivery in rural areas.
That was changed by the late member, Dan McKenzie, who led a group of Tory backbenchers to raise a kerfuffle in the Tory caucus.
Apart from that the corporate plan that Canada Post presented to the government was approved lock, stock, and barrel. That includes the shut-down of post offices in urban areas. That includes the closure of all 5,221 rural post offices in Canada. That is all part of that plan. We on this side of the House did not invent that.
The postmasters and the assistants' association did not invent that.

And neither did Jean-Claude Parrot, nor his union, nor the Letter Carriers Union which already existed at the time. Mr. Speaker, the government must admit it was responsible for this plan. It was the government that gave Canada Post these guidelines. And of course, lest we forget, there is a minister responsible for the Canada Post Corporation. I repeat: responsible.

The government says: "Look how smart we are. Canada Post generates profit". All right. Let us say there is the odd Canadian who still believes that this government is smart. An unlikely proposition given the popularity of the government across the way. Nevertheless, there could be the odd Canadian-there is the odd Canadian who believes that Elvis Presley is still alive, so nothing is impossible- who still believes that the Tories are smart.
Let me tell those misguided few, whatever number there may be, that this is how it works. The 1989-90 annual report of Canada Post is a good example. The member who is heckling across the way, the member for Laval East, said a while ago: "Isn't it Canada Post which gave us $149 million in corporate profits, therefore aren't we great?"

subtopic: POSTAL SERVICES CONTINUATION ACT, 1991 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Let us look at what they have done to labour relations. My distinguished colleague from Essex-Kent has pointed out very astutely-he is always very astute, of course-that Canada Post has profit, any profit, simply because it is two years behind in paying increases to its employees. Small wonder. If I owed you or anyone else money, and I did not pay it, that is money that I would have more than had I paid my debts. That is the situation that they are in as well and it is something that people forget to say. Of course, it is Tories who usually forget to say that.
Let's talk about labour relations at Canada Post. We have heard all the horror stories in that regard. You will remember the Liberal task force on labour relations at Canada Post.
My colleagues from Essex-Kent, Kenora-Rainy River, Mississauga, a number of others and I went to various regions of this countiy. We talked to ordinary Canadians and postal workers as well about the labour relations of Canada Post.
We heard of everything from threats to sexual harassment to everything else going on inside that corporation against employees of the corporation by people in authority. It was just terrible. It was a horror story, the kind of which the United Nations deals with.
Let me give you a fine example of how Canada Post treats people. I brought this letter to the attention of the public before. It is dated December 1986 and it is a letter sent to an employee of Canada Post in the Vancouver mail processing plant.
October 28, 1991

I will say the name of the employee simply because the postal union has made this name public in the past. The letter is addressed to one L. Chu. Listen to this, Mr. Speaker.
The letter talks about this employee who is a real bad person according to management because he has a terrible attendance record. Listen to the facts. It says as follows: "For your information, in December of 1985, you booked off sick on one occasion for a total of one day. One reason that you missed this much work may be that you have overworked yourself.
In December of 1985, you worked 11 hours of overtime. Perhaps this year you should limit the amount of overtime that you work so that your health is not adversely affected".
The letter goes on like that with this kind of nonsense as if an employee who misses one day a month should be reprimanded. An employee who does 11 hours of overtime in a month is about the same as Parliament sitting an extra five minutes.
It is normal but this is the way they treat people. This is the way they treat people inside that corporation. I have cases and cases of such instances in a binder that I have here. I have literally three inches thick of horror stories and that does not even count the backlog of 110,000 grievances that we have right now before the corporation.

Mr. Speaker, I realize that some members across the way will say not all the complaints and grievances of the postal workers are well founded. That may be true. But
110,000	can't be all wrong! A substantial number of those cases are certainly true, are certainly genuine, and Mr. Speaker, they certainly have complaints and grievances that deserve to get a hearing.

Let me give a few instances. Last Friday I raised the case in this House of one Huguette Perrier of Dalkeith, Ontario, in my riding.
Mrs. Perrier was delivering the mail under a rural contract. She picks up the mail at the post office, sorts it out and delivers it on the concession. This person is 65 years old and a widow. She had been doing the job nine
Government Orders
years, since her husband died. Her husband was doing it before that for 15 years.
Between the husband and wife, they had been delivering the mail on that rural route for 24 years. Do you know what they did this year? They put out the job for tender and she lost it because of $1,500.

Meanwhile, the government opposite gave the president of the Canada Post Corporation a salary increase of $131,250! That is not his salary, just a salary increase, Mr. Speaker, adding up to a grand total of $370,000, if I remember correctly.

I have another case. Unfortunately, I cannot name this next individual because I don't have her permission. But I have a person who works in a post office in my riding, a woman again, who phoned me. Most of them are women by the way, 83 per cent of the people who work in rural post offices in Canada are women and the government should remember that. It seldom does. This woman works in a post office and has worked there for some time. She was sick and needed surgery. She had an operation and obtained a medical certificate prior to leaving. When she came back she received a letter from her superior cancelling her sick leave retroactively from the date it was awarded and deducting from her pay cheque a reimbursement of the sick leave that she took.
I intervened on her behalf and had the nonsense cancelled. Of course they ceased to collect money from her and they gave her back that which they had already collected.
That is the way people are treated in that corporation. When these cases were happening in my constituency, I got wind of a manager at Canada Post who had seemingly nothing to do. This person was phoning post offices in my riding and asking postmasters to remove the picture of the Queen from the post office. That happened in Hawkesbury, L'Orignal and Vankleek Hill. Who asked for this? No one that we could ever determine. It was simply someone in management at the post office who had nothing better to do than to concoct a scheme for himself or herself to have the Queen's picture removed

October 28, 1991
Government Orders
from post offices. Now what on earth is that supposed to accomplish?
When I protested about this to the officials of Canada Post, I told them that the day we decide to change the head of state of our country, it sure won't be a flunkey inside the postal system who will make that decision. It won't be a post office manager, it will be the Parliament of Canada after consultation with the people of Canada and no one else. But why did that particular manager make that decision? I never got an answer from Canada Post. The Queen's picture is back in the post offices finally. In one case it took about four months to put back the frame that took 30 seconds to take off, but they finally did it.
Why don't they just deliver the mail? Does that sound so hard?
In rural Canada, Canada Post got into this binge of shutting down rural post offices. Now here is how it went about doing it: It decided to shut down rural post offices if and when the postmaster died or retired. Now, in Canada Post jargon that is referred to as the "natural opportunity criteria". Here is how it works:
If a postmaster dies, that is natural and therefore there is a natural opportunity created, so you shut down the post office. That is how the natural opportunity criteria works. If the postmaster retires, he or she has aged and reached the age of retirement, ageing is also natural therefore the natural opportunity criteria has been met again. So that is how that works too.
So you shut down the post office and you franchise it out. There is no more post office and the mail is sorted 15, 20, 30 miles away. It is brought in weather permitting, and then of course people go and get it outside in supermailboxes that freeze in winter. That is known as improved service.
The way the criteria for this improved service works is the following:

Whether the post office in question made a profit or a loss was not a factor. There probably are examples where a rural post office makes a substantial profit, but Canada Post is not interested in such mundane matters. It is interested in closing a post office if it feels like it or if it seems like a good time to do it, without always considering there may be some very good reasons for keeping the post office open. No, it closes them regardless, to the
extent that we have lost about 2,000 post offices in rural areas in Canada, if I am not mistaken.
Some time ago we appointed in this country a Postal Services Review Committee. This Postal Services Review Committee was appointed by the government and led by Mr. Alan Marchment. This committee was to make recommendations on future postal increases, the quality of management and all kinds of things at Canada Post.
Guess what happened to this postal review committee? The committee was supposed to have been transformed into a board. There was legislation presented in this House. It died on the Order Paper. The government never proceeded with the legislation and never reintroduced it. This postal review committee and the future postal review board was to be the watchdog of the post office, a form of CRTC of the post office, if I can call it that. It died on the Order Paper.
Not only that but when the Postal Service Review Committee brought forward its report, the government read the report, did not like the contents and fired the committee because it did not like what it heard.

This is what the Review Committee on Canada Post recommended in its first and last report, after which it was disbanded by the government opposite. Some of its recommendations were:
That Canada Post examine the possibility of extending home mail delivery in urban areas.
Second, that Canada Post review its program for closing rural post offices.
Third, prevent deregulation of the majority of services offered by Canada Post.
These recommendations were made by the Review Committee on Canada Post. I myself appeared before the committee to discuss these three points and a number of other points, and I did so on behalf of my colleagues in the Liberal party who told me those were the kind of recommendations we needed. The Marchment Committee obviously agreed, since the committee adopted them. However, the committee was then disbanded thanks to the Minister responsible for the Canada Post Corporation, who is sitting right across from

me, Mr. Speaker. I can see him quite plainly, the Minister responsible for the Canada Post Corporation!

The question today is not whether we support the government. The question is: Do we need a postal service in this country? Any support for this bill should not by anyone be mistaken as supporting the Tories, the government or even the Prime Minister, most of all the minister responsible for Canada Post.
In conclusion, I say to the government across the way that when there are problems at Canada Post a mea culpa is needed on its part. It has created the mess we are in now.

If it was, I would like to know specifically in what respect.
Second, I would appreciate knowing from the hon. member whether he embraces a particular position in the dispute. Does he embrace without reservation the position of the postal union?
Third, what would the Canada Post deficit be today if the corporate plan had not been invoked and if we had proceeded along the merry path the previous administration had set us upon?

I do not want to be misunderstood on this because I do not believe there have been many cases of law breaking or even suggestions that there has been law breaking on the picket lines, but there were suggestions during the previous strike, the strike by Public Service Alliance of Canada members, and so I ask it in the broadest sense, when strikers are seen or are believed to have broken the
Government Orders
law is it the role of the police to keep the peace or to apprehend or arrest suspected law breakers?
Finally, I heard a very tantalizing observation by the hon. member at the conclusion of his speech when he seemed to suggest that he might be going to vote for this bill, and I would like to ask him whether that is what he meant.

I have illustrated the plan to remove rural mail delivery save on county and regional roads. That is another example. That one was changed. There was the plan for the supermailboxes that do not open but freeze up in winter. Ask anyone who owns a supermailbox that will not open and freezes up in winter how great those contraptions are.

I was also asked by the member across the way what the profit would be if that corporate plan had not been adopted. Mr. Speaker, before addressing what was said by the hon. member for Glengarry-Prescott- Russell, I would like to set the record straight, because the Liberals have a terrible habit of getting figures all mixed up. First of all, the president has not been with Canada Post for 11 years. There were two presidents: Michael Warren, from 1981 to 1985, and Donald Lander, from 1985 until now. The hon. member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell says he knows that. Too bad he did not say so before. I had to go and look it up.
Before, in 1981, Canada Post was administered by ministers and public servants-by bureaucrats. There were plenty of those! However there was also an annual deficit that varied from $400 to $600 million. Taxpayers are aware of this, and they don't want any part of it. I would prefer a profit of $200 million and getting my mail.
The hon. member said earlier:

"We sold the assets, that is why you made money." The important thing in this world is to get the mail delivered before two or three weeks, to get the mail like it is today, in two or three days. We have the best service
in the world now. Canada Post is one of the best services in the world. That is what the business people want in my area.
If my friend is looking for more names, the hon. member from the Montreal area was a postmaster general in the days when the mail was not delivered very much. We did not do a lot when it was freezing in the winter time, I admit that, but we had a $600 million deficit because it was administered by the bureaucrats and the minister.
What I would like to know from my hon. colleague is what is important, the colour of the trucks or delivery of the mail? It is to get the mail through in a few days, as soon as possible, so businesses can get their mail, the senior people can get their cheques and all this.

I also wanted to tell the hon. member that if things are that bad, if this government is as bad as all that, how come Canada Post is one the best postal services in the world today? How come our businesses are satisfied? In 1984, when I was elected-and I am about to conclude my remarks-we saw trucks run by all kinds of companies, like Purolator, but not by Canada Post. Today, we hardly see any. At the time, Canada Post was losing contracts to private businesses, but today, it is a private business.

subtopic: POSTAL SERVICES CONTINUATION ACT, 1991 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to first comment on the last comment of the member from Laval East because he made reference in his questions to the previous speaker about delivery of the mail being the most important thing with Canada Post.
I would just like to refer him to an article in the Globe and Mail recently that said "Canada Post, Canada's largest Crown corporation, should be a dream operation. It has no competitors on its most lucrative product, first-class mail, renamed letter mail a couple of years ago when it was decided first class could no longer accurately describe the service. The price of a stamp is raised through an Order in Council, a cabinet decree that by-passes public scrutiny, and the government requires that private couriers charge three times as much as Canada Post to deliver a letter within the country".
Is this the same government that is now standing in this House and speaking in great glowing terms of how it believes that Canada Post is operating as a private corporation? Let us at least stay close to the truth when we are discussing Canada Post in terms of what Canada Post is.
I rise feeling again saddened in this House. This is the ninth piece of back-to-work legislation that we have seen from the government since the Conservatives have been in power. It is the fourth piece in the past year. It is the fourth while the current Minister of Labour has been in his position.
Parliament is becoming a labour court. Collective bargaining in the public sector has been reduced to being
Government Orders
dependent on back-to-work legislation, not on collective bargaining. It is symptomatic that there are problems with how government and Crown corporations operate when dealing with their workers.
It is the policies of this government with regard to Canada Post that have precipitated this dispute. The zeal for privatization has meant a reduced level of service, a worsening of labour-management relations and closures of both rural and urban post offices.
We have heard hon. members from the other side of the House standing up and saying: "We must order these workers back to work". Let there me no mistake, CUPW did not issue its 24-hour notice until after the Minister of Labour rose in this House and introduced legislation for continuation of service in Canada Post.
We are not talking here at this moment of back-to-work legislation, we are talking about pre-emptive legislation that puts into place before a labour dispute, before a walk-out, legislation that requires those workers to stay on the job. It seems more to me to be about the removal of the right to strike than back-to-work legislation.
Closures of rural post offices and of urban post offices have meant a loss of 14,000 full time jobs. Those were well paying jobs and only a fraction of those closures from which private postal outlets were created have gone to unionized workers making a decent salary. Most of them have gone to corner groceries and convenience stores, drug stores and those workers are low-paid and often have very few if any fringe benefits.
We have had hon. members get up on the other side of the House and talk about overpaid postal workers. I would reiterate there is nothing in this country that should make one worker ashamed of drawing a decent salary for a decent day's pay. Of the people I have been in contact with at Canada Post, I do not know anyone who does not deliver a good day's work for a good day's pay.
Canada Post is firing workers at three times the rate of the federal Public Service and of most private sector work places. Privatization is firmly rooted in this government's strategy of fulfilling the wish of corporate Canada. In fact the BCNI and the Fraser Institute have been referred to by the other side of the House in setting the agenda for Canada Post with little if any consideration

October 28, 1991
Government Orders
for the needs of Canadian people, and certainly for the needs of those who work for Canada Post.
Privatization there is no doubt, because of where Canada postal stations are being opened, is hurting women workers the most. In fact the trend that is being accelerated of last hired first fired is leaving women unemployed from Canada Post in ever increasing numbers. In rural post offices 82 per cent of the workers who worked for Canada Post are or were women. I want to talk a bit about Canada Post as it is reflected in my area of Canada. My riding of Mission-Coquitlam is what one would call a suburban-urban-rural riding. Some people commute regularly. Some people work in the soft fruit industry and farming. Other people in fact work in communities in my riding and actually work in the area in the forest industry and fishing.
For the commuter the closure of post offices has become a nightmare. For the elderly and disabled in my riding the supermailboxes-and I use that term with a somewhat puzzled look on my face-are a horror and a nightmare. To ask elderly people in communities like mine in Canada where there is limited transportation and where there are limits in terms of streetlighting to go to supermailboxes and pick up their mail is just beyond comprehension. Then they are told they are getting improved service and it is a supermailbox.
The hon. member who spoke just before me talked about freezing locks. We do not get quite as much cold weather on the west coast of British Columbia as some parts of Canada, but we too have problems with freezing mailboxes. We also have problems because of the amount of precipitation and rain we have with rusted mailboxes, where the locks cannot be opened because they have rusted shut. I do not think that that could be called super service.
Another thing we are faced with is terrible messes on the ground of soggy flyers, et cetera, that people leave behind which have to be waded through, not to mention people who walk their dogs to get their mail and whose
dogs do one thing while they are getting their mail and others are left to walk through it.
Supermailboxes are not a lot of fun, and for Canada Post to continually tell us that through this we are getting improved service is rather insulting.
In addition, you get a card to pick up a parcel in my riding. On a number of occasions I have received a card myself and have gone to the location where it says I should go to pick up my parcel, only to discover that those people got fed up and do not have the franchise for Canada Post any more and I have to go somewhere else but they are not sure where. I have to go to the post office to find out where I have to go to pick up my parcel. That is a regular routine happening in Mission- Coquitlam and I am sure it is not unique to that particular riding.
Last winter we had an unusual amount of snow in my riding and there are a number of rural delivery routes. I had all over the Christmas and January season endless complaints from rural route people who for weeks on end, not days, and in one case well over a month, did not get mail delivery because in fact the new people who had the new contracts could not keep up and could not cope with the weather on the roads. Yet for years when we previously had inclement weather before Canada Post had implemented its new super service we had no difficulty in those same areas where people had been receiving their mail for 25 years.
Last August when the rotating strikes began in my riding the workers said they would not deliver flyers on the last day or the day the cheques were supposed to go out, unless they were given the opportunity to deliver old age pension cheques as well. Canada Post refused to give the old age pension cheques to the carriers.
When I called Canada Post and inquired as to why this was so, the response was: "We are fulfilling our commitment to our customer". When asked who "our customer" is, the Government of Canada was the customer. When asked why, when they had a memo of which I had a copy that said the mail should be delivered on or before Wednesday and it was after Wednesday, the cheques
October 28, 1991

were not being delivered, I got the answer: "We are fulfilling our commitment to our customer".
When we have said that they want to deliver the mail, they want to ensure that people are not left high and dry without their cheques, and Canada Post is refusing to deliver those cheques even though there is not a strike in place, that begs the question of attitude. It begs the question of the attitude of Canada Post to its workers. That, I would suggest, is very much at the root of the reason why we are even discussing this legislation today in this House.
There is a backlog of over 100,000 union grievances filed by postal workers against their employers-100,000 grievances. The hon. member for Saint-Jean says withdraw them and we would not have a problem. My goodness, I am finding it really hard to keep my language parliamentary here. We are talking about 100,000 grievances. Even if half of them were bum grievances, that means there is still 50,000 legitimate grievances and it is high time that we started addressing the problem here.
CUPW spends a quarter of its annual budget fighting on behalf of its members with regard to grievances. God knows, if CUPW is spending a quarter of its budget, how many bucks is Canada Post spending to fight those workers through the hiring of expensive lawyers, taking these grievances to arbitration, or even end-running these grievances. It is a waste. If in fact labour relations were on a decent, even keel and there was respect for the workers in the work place, we would not be facing
100,000	grievances.
Workers in my riding and in other ridings I have been told of are being harassed constantly with spot checks of personal belongings, phone calls at home while they are off sick to determine if they will be returning to work or if they could assume other duties, including sick calls for night shift workers in the wee hours of the morning.
I have a large number of CUPW members in my riding who have told me of the harassment and intimidation that goes on daily in their work places. They told me of colleagues who have had to take time off because of the stress of constant surveillance and constant harassment. This is not cost effective. This is not good private sector behaviour. This is not the kind of behaviour that is going to produce a grand corporate profit, but in fact the kind of behaviour that leads us into the kind of discussion we are having today.
Government Orders
If Canada Post were really concerned about it being efficient and effective, it would spend more time and more resources improving its labour relations in the work place instead of trying to convince the rest of us that it really does provide a decent service when everyone knows that it is simply not the case.
There is another factor. I cannot tell you, Mr. Speaker, how many times Canada Post workers have said to me: "I have always wanted to do a good job. I take pride in my ability and my skill, but I have been deprived by Canada Post of the ability to work with dignity because people are so angry at the corporation and I am the first line that people see and I get it from the customer who is dissatisfied".
One of the things that most members of this House could agree with is that they probably have file drawers full of complaints from constituents regarding Canada Post. They are complaints about changes that have a lot more to do with the Tory corporate agenda than with the priorities of Canadians who want and need a good postal service, a lot more to do with a corporate agenda than anything to do with the needs of people who serve their employer and sell their employer their working hours every working day of the week.
Some of the statistics regarding Canada Post are truly frightening. Since January 1986 Canada Post has closed over 1,160 federally owned and operated post offices. Canada Post's stated plan is to close all public post offices by 1996. This will cost 14,000 decent paying unionized jobs, and then the government wonders why workers who work at Canada Post are just a bit upset.
As I said earlier, there are 100,000 outstanding grievances with Canada Post. From 1981 to 1984, five workers a month were fired. In 1991 the average was 59 workers a month who were fired by Canada Post. According to The Ottawa Citizen, Canada Post is firing staff two to four times more frequently than the federal Public Service and most private sector employers in Ontario. A wonderful, wonderful labour relations record for Canada Post.
There used to be a guarantee that there would be door-to-door delivery to communities with more than
2,000	points of call. Not any more. In fact in my community whole communities have fought the changes to Canada Post. They have fought the closures of their post offices. The whole community fought to be rid of supermailboxes and get the same kind of service on this

October 28, 1991
Government Orders
side of the street as their neighbours got on that side of the street.
What has the response from Canada Post been? No matter what you say to somebody, when you call Canada Post at the top levels to try to get some answers you get the corporate line: "We are committed to providing more service to Canadians". No matter who you speak to, no matter what the issue is and no matter what kind of information you are trying to get, you get the corporate answer of: "We are committed to better serving Canadians".
This is the outcome. Canada Post has purchased a corporate box in Toronto's SkyDome for $250,000. Canada Post's health and safety record is so bad that it had 10,036 debilitating work place injuries. In fact it was only exceeded by Devco. The Cape Breton Development Corporation had more injuries on a per capita basis. This is the Canada Post that is now unable to conclude a collective agreement with the union. Now the Minister of Labour comes to this House and introduces legislation that is not back-to-work legislation but the removal of the right to strike legislation because it pre-empts in fact a strike even taking place.
In conclusion, I would say that this government has a responsibility, albeit it is a Crown corporation it is dealing with, to make it very clear to Canada Post that corporate industrial relations have to improve so that we are not faced with this every time we go to the bargaining table.

Mr. Speaker, I rise today to speak on a matter which this House has heard over, and over, and over again, both from me and from other

members on this side. I refer to the future of Canada's world class port, the port of Halifax.

Six times I have risen to speak in debate concerning the port and six times the phalanx of government backbenchers replied that there was no problem, that the seven container lines that left in 1991 would come back when circumstances permitted.
As the member for Halifax, I brought a private members' motion, M-540 before the committee and then this House. The government responded by voting against a modest proposal to change the way CN rail does business between Halifax and central Canada.
Two Standing Orders later and still no action from this government.
I rise again today to ask the government that preaches competitiveness to us on a daily basis to please, for once, let us compete. I demand on behalf of the out of work dockworkers and the silent piers of Halifax that this government wake up. Bring the ships back.
This government, by Order in Council, can make CN rail re-establish our lifeline to central Canada. No more studies. No more discussions over cocktails. Implement the proposals of the secret report, the report the government will not show us. As long as it goes on, as it goes on today, I will rise in this House again and again and again until the government realizes that it is throwing away the key to trade in the 21st century and the key to prosperity in the port of Halifax.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate again the hon. member's tenacity in this question. I am pleased again to respond to her. I think we are making progress.
Let us first address some facts. There have been some problems in the port this year and some business has

October 28, 1991
Adjournment Debate
been lost. The hon. member should also mention that the port has previously set new records for the number of 20 foot equivalent unit containers. We on this side of the House would like to see a new record set every year but that cannot always happen.
When there is a downturn in traffic everyone is rightly concerned and all the parties work together to make sure every action is taken to restore the traffic. That is why Canada Ports Corporation as a federal agency is trying to facilitate a longer term co-operation between the container ports and the railways to enhance the attractiveness of Canadian container routings in general and has worked with the port of Halifax in particular.
That is why Canadian National Railway and the province developed an agreement for the funding of lease and purchase of double stack rail cars. That is why the city of Halifax has come to the assistance of the port by significantly trimming the taxes on the container terminals. That is why the port has made several concessions that are directly aimed at improving the port's attractiveness to foreign ocean liners.
I will give some examples: Capping of berthage charges; wharfage discount inventive on all traffic originating in or destined for the United States; establishing a maximum limit to the number of times a liner must pay harbour dues; and as well, certain other port tariffs have been frozen for two years.
The hon. member has been asking for a copy of the Ports Canada Container Study. I am informed that the corporation will be releasing a report to interested parties very shortly, perhaps as early as this week.
More important than the physical release of the report, though, is that the report will be the basis of important discussions at meetings with the container ports, and their marine communities. These regional meetings will provide an opportunity for discussion and feedback not only on the competitive issues facing the ports but on the potential strategies to maintain our competitive position in the world transportation system.
If the member can share with the world the way to solve the problem of over-capacity on the high seas, she will have joined the rest of us who are working to promote this great port.

subtopic: SITTING RESUMED 4.50 P.M. The House resumed at 4.50 p.m.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on October 9 I asked the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources what he was going to do to help the mining industry.
I pointed out to him that the mining industry in northern Ontario is in dire need. I informed him of the approximately 1,000 jobs that were lost last year in the Timmins area alone. The minister spoke of current negotiations for mineral development agreements between the federal government and its provincial counterparts.
The mining industry and those who depend on its livelihood would welcome just about any good news at this point. They need a firm commitment from this government that it will do all that is possible to ensure this industry's future.
I would just like to quote from a Canadian minerals yearbook, published and authored by Energy, Mines and Resources, Canada. This document refers to the year 1990 and I quote:
Lower commodity prices in 1990, combined with higher interest rates and a strong Canadian dollar, resulted in poorer financial performance for most producers.
The financial results for the first three quarters of the year gave indications that earnings for the full year could end up being as low as half the earnings of 1989.
I think that is an area that still exists today. It is an area that this government could be looking into. We have mentioned before that the Canadian dollar is too high. We have mentioned that Canadian interest rates are too high and I think that is one of the solutions that could be looked at by the minister.
Another area that the minister could look at was put forward by my colleague from Churchill and is the establishment of a national mining reserve fund. In his proposal he outlined the fact that Statistics Canada figures indicate that the federal government benefits from the mining industry. It received $1.5 billion in federal revenue from it.
He only asked that some of that money be set aside for the future to provide more security for those living in the mining communities. I think it is a fair and reasonable approach and should be very seriously considered by this government.
October 28, 1991

In conclusion, I would like to ask the minister once again if he would look into the future and think about protecting this country from further losses of revenue by letting this industry die.

subtopic: SITTING RESUMED 4.50 P.M. The House resumed at 4.50 p.m.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to express my dissatisfaction with the minister of Indian Affairs' response to my question of September 18 concerning the failure of the Dene land claims negotiations in the Northwest Territories.
Adjournment Debate
The failure resulted from the government's refusal to proceed with the land claims settlement unless the Dene agreed to the extinguishment of their aboriginal title. With the collapse of a comprehensive agreement the government then proceeded to negotiate with those tribes which were willing to abandon aboriginal rights and title in exchange for a land claims settlement.
The minister responsible for Canada's race laws and his staff at Indian Affairs are treating aboriginal people with the same colonialist Machiavellian divide and conquer approach that has been the hallmark of Canada's relations with its aboriginal people over the last 200 years.
In fact the minister was asked a question in the House today about the Algonquin land claims proposal. The minister led the questioner to believe that his department had funded land claims research for the Algonquin people to the tune of over $.5 million. In fact that funding went to a single band and the research was rejected by all but two of the Algonquin bands. In spite of that the government refuses to fund a joint research proposal that is supported by the majority of the Algonquin people. It is another example of the ministry's divide and conquer tactics.
The final example is the Lubicon nation which has attempted to bargain in good faith with the government for many years, in each case to be met with stonewalling and subversion of the talks. In fact the government even established a new band, the Woodland Cree and has settled its claims on the government's terms over part of the Lubicon lands. Now we hear that the government is intriguing among the Lubicon Lake people to establish another band which will claim another part of Lubicon lands, and again settle on the government's terms.
I do not blame the aboriginal people for their willingness to abandon some of their rights and title in order to achieve a land claim settlement. Many of these people are desperate and feel forced to sacrifice their rights in order to obtain the land and resource base they need to provide the basic necessities for their people. I blame the minister responsible for Canada's race laws and his department, who continue to use the most cynical, deceitful, divide and conquer tactics to deprive our

Adjournment Debate
aboriginal people of rights which are supposedly protected in the Canadian Constitution.

speakeroldname: Mrs. Barbara Sparrow (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: SITTING RESUMED 4.50 P.M. The House resumed at 4.50 p.m.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to respond to the hon. member for Comox-Alberni.
The recent approval by the Gwitch'in of their comprehensive land claim agreement is proof of progress, and progress in the right direction. The Gwitch'in claim was under negotiation as part of the Dene-Metis claim for over 10 years before it became a regional claim in November of last year.
With the decision of the Dene and Chief Bill Erasmus not to proceed with ratification, the Government of Canada agreed to proceed on a regional basis with those groups which were pressing us to finalize their claim settlements. In the Gwitch'in ratification vote, 91 per cent of eligible voters voted; 94 per cent of those voting approved the agreement. This is truly a remarkable show of determination by this particular group and we prefer to negotiate an agreement and then abide by the decision the Indian people themselves make.
Under the agreement, the Gwitch'in will own 8,658 square miles of land, including surface rights for 27 per cent. They will receive a non-taxable payment of $75 million. Other benefits will include guaranteed wildlife harvesting rights and guaranteed representation of public-government boards to manage the wildlife, land and water and the environmental reviews.
This agreement, embraced almost unanimously by the Gwitch'in, is based upon the Dene-Metis agreement initialled in April of 1990. The Dene-Metis could also have voted on the agreement, but instead in July 1990 their joint assembly decided not to allow a vote on it. The Gwitch'in walked out of the assembly before the vote and the Sahtu region abstained.
This agreement is a clear indication of the government's commitment to accelerate the settlement on aboriginal claims and to adopt new and innovative approaches to their resolution.
In conclusion, the Gwitch'in agreed to exchange their unwritten aboriginal rights for written treaty rights. The president of the Gwitch'in tribal council himself said; "We don't feel we are extinguishing anything."

subtopic: SITTING RESUMED 4.50 P.M. The House resumed at 4.50 p.m.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on October 4, I requested the Minister of National Health and Welfare to underline his department's policy on the sleeping drug Triazolan, better known by the brand name Halcion. This drug is the most popular sedative in Canada and has been prescribed to some 34 million people in this country since 1978.
My question to the minister was simple: Since the minister has indicated his department has agreed to move very quickly, within hours, if just cause were found to ban it in Canada, can the minister tell the House today-that was on October 4-what decision has he made?
The reason behind the question was a growing suspicion of the capability of the Health Protection Branch because I am afraid it is not equipped to anticipate dangers to the public health. This question was of a vein that had been pursued by me on other occasions, on other matters including the Meme breast implant, the heart drug Betaloc and with Sudafed and now with Triazolan.
I want to be reassured and I want Canadians to be reassured that the Health Protection Branch has the fortitude and power to act quickly, concisely and always in the best interests of Canadians when threats arise. I want Canadians to be reassured that the government is giving the Health Protection Branch enough financial and human resources to do its job.
I believe the threat from Halcion or triazolan does not come purely from the drug itself which is apparently under extensive clinical trials in order to have its use approved. I think the problem rises from societal and administrative problems which when coupled result in the over-prescription of this drug to thousands.
The monograph on the drug states that the dosage should be discontinued after 21 consecutive days despite the fact that many patients have been on the drug for months and sometimes even years.
I can understand how side effects which typically affect about 5 per cent of the triazolan users can cause more adverse responses if the drug is not used properly. It is just such an abuse that should be regulated and monitored by the Health Protection Branch. Within the HPD there is a separate area called the Adverse Drug Reac-
October 28, 1991

tion Reporting Program. This body should been given adequate resources to do its job.
Britain and the United States have shown concern about this drug and I would believe that the minister should not take weeks to make a decision on the safety of a drug affecting millions in our country.
If agencies like the Health Protection Branch and the Adverse Drug Reaction Reporting Program were given a new mandate for protection and better funding, it follows they could better protect and serve Canadians.
I believe that Canadians should closely watch and monitor Canadians. Is there abuse of this sleeping drug in our society? Is it being commonly over-prescribed to patients who are female, aged and in long-term care facilities? If so, why? Why has the Health Protection Branch not reacted sooner? I hope today the minister can respond to my concerns with more than the usual: "We have struck a committee of venerable experts to study the issue".
I hope the minister will have a reply today, right now, on whether the decision on triazolan's safety has been decided and whether a directive to this effect has been sent to consumers, to pharmacies and to other health care providers.

speakeroldname: Mrs. Barbara Sparrow (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: SITTING RESUMED 4.50 P.M. The House resumed at 4.50 p.m.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to respond to my colleague's question.
On October 2, 1991, the Medicines Control Agency, which is the drug regulatory authority in the United Kingdom, suspended the product licence for Halcion or triazolan for a three month period.
This action was based upon a new analysis of safety data which the U.K. authorities interpreted as suggesting that risks associated with triazolan outweighed its benefits. Some countries, namely Finland, Norway, Jamaica, Bermuda and Argentina followed suit.
Officials of Health and Welfare Canada immediately contacted both the U.K. officials to request the data upon which they had based their decision and Upjohn Canada to request all the information that the company had provided to the U.K. department.
The department officials also met with senior officials from Upjohn on October 7, 1991. The conclusion drawn by Health and Welfare Canada was that, based on a
Adjournment Debate
preliminary assessment, there was no evidence of new risks at the recommended doses.
A more detailed assessment is being done based on documentation obtained from the U.K. regulatory authorities as well as from the Upjohn people. We hope to have that information within the next short period of time.
I would like to say that a similar position was taken by the U.S., by Sweden and by the committee for proprietary medicinal products at a meeting in Brussels on October 14 to October 16.
The CPMP made recommendations and its recommendations with regard to information are already in place in Canada. These include labelling information, informing physicians and consumers that triazolan should not be used longer than the 21 day period consecutively and that the lowest effective dose should be used, particularly with our elderly people.
I just have to say once more that with a panel of experts we will be reviewing this and we will come forward within a short period of time.

subtopic: SITTING RESUMED 4.50 P.M. The House resumed at 4.50 p.m.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, once again I am a bit like my colleague from Halifax. I have been on my feet 14 times since this House resumed in September and mostly on the subject of control of the cod stocks in Newfoundland, the subject that is making fishermen angry. It is making them demoralized and it is causing a lot of anger in our caucus.
When you stand up and talk about it, it sounds reasonably simple, but somehow we cannot seem to be able to get the message across to the government or to anybody else that despite all the rules and regulations, we are the only country in the world that I am aware of that gives away to foreigners and allows them to take, through whatever means, the very resources upon which people depend for their livelihood.
Just a quick background on this so that we are all talking from the same text if you like. In 1978, a year after we established a 200-mile zone, the Northwest Atlantic Fisheries Organization which was established as a result of this, agreed that Canada would manage the

October 28, 1991
Adjournment Debate
cod stocks that I am speaking about essentially in 2J,3K-L, which are NAFO designated areas essentially off the north and east cost of of Newfoundland and Labrador, even though it was recognized as a transboundary stock, on the grounds that only a very small part of the stock was normally present outside the 200-mile limit and that for only a very small part of the year and also because of the vital importance of the stock to the coastal state.
That existed in 1978, but somehow in the last few years things have changed. Right now, NAFO does the scientific assessment of the 2J,3K-L stocks and, furthermore, it continues to establish quotas to be fished outside the 200-mile limit.
NAFO is toothless as it is devoid of teeth. Its moral authority counts for less than nothing in this world of dog eat dog and nations of the European community, for example, may through the simple expedient of filing a protest against the total allowable catch, which I will call TAC, set by NAFO free themselves from any obligation to be bound by it.
In practice in particular such nations as Spain and Portugal habitually ignore scientific advice. They flaunt their defiance of controversial strategies and they limit their catches only by the capacity of their fishing fleets.
Mr. Speaker, some examples: in 1986 Canada established a northern cod TAC of 266,000 tonnes. NAFO proposed the TAC for the European community countries of 36,000 tonnes to be taken from the nose and the tail of the bank in which these countries reported landings were approximately 100,000 tonnes. Can you imagine?
Let me take you up to last year. In 1990 the TAC was
190,000	tonnes. The NAFO quota was set at 15,377. They allocated themselves unilaterally 59,400 and they took 97,750. In other words, they took the same last year when the total allowable catch was 190,000 tonnes as they took back in 1986 when the TAC was 20 per cent or 30 per cent larger.
In the context of international irresponsibility this amounts, in the eyes of Newfoundlanders and I hope Canadians, to outright piracy. The mandate of the Canadian Minister of Fisheries and Oceans cannot be properly executed. There is only one way it can be done, and this recommendation was made by the Independent
Review of the State of the Northern Cod Stocks back in February last year. It is not just the member for Bonavis-ta-Trinity-Conception. I am quoting what is considered to be a very authoritative document. Its recommendation reads, and I will quote it: "Ideally we believe that control should be exercised by a single authority and that authority should be Canada".
In conclusion, turning to the example of Iceland back in 1975, when other countries including Great Britain decided to take them on Icelanders declared that this was a resource that was essential to their livelihood. They brought out their gunboats to substantiate their belief in this and the fact that they would take control of their own resources. I wish to heaven's name we would consider doing the same thing.

speakeroldname: Mr. Lee Richardson (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: SITTING RESUMED 4.50 P.M. The House resumed at 4.50 p.m.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member has alleged that foreign vessels overfishing in the northwest Atlantic take almost as much fish as Canadians receive in allocations. He has also implied that the government is not serious about proper conservation of fish and the viability of the Atlantic fishing industiy.
While I appreciate the member's sincerity, both of these are far from correct. Groundfishing quotas allocated to Canadian fishermen in 1991 totalled 816 tonnes, including some 49,000 tonnes of groundfish stocks managed by NAFO. This total of Canadian quotas which are fished by Canadians mainly inside the Canadian 200-mile zone is about four times greater than even the highest estimate of what foreign vessels are catching outside 200 miles. The problem of foreign overfishing outside 200 miles is real and serious but should not be blown into fantasy proportions.
The other members of NAFO, including the European Community, received groundfish allocations from NAFO totalling some 81,000 tonnes in 1991. The foreign vessels fish their NAFO quotas mostly outside the Canadian fishing zone, on the Grand Banks and on the Flemish Cap. These are NAFO-managed stocks.
The problem of foreign overfishing does not occur inside Canada's 200-mile zone. It does not occur because of the quotas set by NAFO outside 200 miles. The overfishing problems occurs only when vessels from several countries choose to fish outside 200 miles in excess of the quotas that are established by NAFO.
October 28, 1991

I am advised that two members of the European Community, Spain and Portugal, as the hon. member has mentioned, are the main overfishing nations and two countries that are not members of NAFO, Panama and Korea, are also major causes of the overfishing problem.
The Government of Canada is very concerned about the overfishing that is taking place in the northwest Atlantic outside the Canadian 200-mile limit and the consequences of this for Atlantic fishing communities, especially in Newfoundland. We have conducted a comprehensive international campaign to eliminate foreign overfishing and are making progress.
The government is making sure people know what is happening in the northwest Atlantic and the consequences of overfishing. Federal and provincial parliamentarians of all parties, technical experts and fishing industry representatives have participated in making this information available.
Canada has also undertaken a legal initiative, including work within the United Nations, to seek a legal basis for international control of high seas fisheries and for
Adjournment Debate
recognition of the special rights and interests of coastal states such as Canada in management and conservation of straddling stocks. Agreement on measures needed to control high seas fisheries is a priority objective for Canada at the United Nations Conference on the Environment and Development.
We have not yet achieved our goals, as the member points out. We know that foreign vessels are still overfishing outside Canada's fishing zone. We will continue our efforts. The government does not intend to jeopardize future success by permitting Canadian fishermen to overfish, whether inside or outside our zone.
